meta.title: Investments in equity securities
meta.summary: Levels of influence, equity securities at fair value through net income, the measurement alternative, the equity method, excess of cost over book value, consolidation and control, and presentation.

videos.title: Influence decides the method
videos.take: Under 20%: fair value; 20–50% with significant influence: equity method; over 50%: consolidate

scenes.say: Bluestem buys shares in two companies: a small stake in its aluminum supplier, and a big one in a paddle maker. Different stakes, different accounting.

scenes.heading: Levels of influence
scenes.say: The method depends on influence. With little or no influence, usually under twenty percent, use fair value with changes in net income. With significant influence, usually twenty to fifty percent, use the equity method. With control, usually over fifty percent, consolidate.

The percentages are guides. A board seat, major transactions between the companies, or shared management can give significant influence at fifteen percent. A forty percent stake may give none if another owner controls everything.
Unlike debt, equity securities don't have an available-for-sale category with OCI. Since 2018, changes in the fair value of equity investments go through net income.
Why switch methods at significant influence? Because an investor that helps steer the investee shares responsibility for its earnings, so it should report its share of them.

scenes.q: Bluestem owns 35% of a company and has two of seven board seats. Method?
scenes.say: Quick check. Bluestem owns thirty-five percent of a company and has two of seven board seats. Which method? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Fair value through net income
videos.take: Record dividends as revenue and remeasure to fair value each period, with changes in net income

scenes.say: Bluestem buys 5,000 shares of its aluminum supplier, a listed company, at $40 a share: a tiny stake.

scenes.heading: Purchase
scenes.say: Bluestem records the investment at cost, $200,000.

scenes.heading: During the year
scenes.say: The supplier pays a $1 dividend: $5,000 of dividend revenue. At year-end the shares trade at $43, worth $215,000: an unrealized holding gain of $15,000.

scenes.heading: Year-end adjustment
scenes.say: The $15,000 gain is recognized in net income. Equity investments are volatile, so this can swing earnings, which some companies dislike.

For shares without a readily determinable fair value, like a stake in a private startup, companies can use a measurement alternative: cost less impairment, adjusted when an orderly transaction in similar shares reveals a price.

scenes.q: Equity securities: cost $90,000; fair value $84,000. Effect on net income?
scenes.say: Quick check. Equity securities: cost ninety thousand; fair value eighty-four thousand. Effect on net income? Pause and pick.

videos.title: The equity method
videos.take: Investment grows with the investor's share of income and shrinks with dividends received

scenes.say: Bluestem buys thirty percent of Northshore Paddle Company for $600,000, and gets two seats on its board.

sub: Record cost, then adjust for the
investor's share of income and dividends
scenes.say: Under the equity method, the investment is recorded at cost, then increased by the investor's share of the investee's income and decreased by dividends received.

scenes.heading: Northshore, 2031
scenes.say: Northshore earns $250,000 and pays $80,000 of dividends. Bluestem records thirty percent of the income, $75,000, as investment income, and its $24,000 share of dividends as a reduction of the investment. The investment ends at $651,000.

scenes.heading: The entries
scenes.say: Income increases the investment. Dividends are a return of part of the investment, not income: counting them as income would let Bluestem's share of earnings be counted twice.

sub: Share of losses reduces the investment,
scenes.say: If Northshore loses money, Bluestem's share reduces the investment, but usually not below zero unless Bluestem has guaranteed Northshore's debts.

scenes.q: 40% investee earns $100,000 and pays $30,000 dividends. Change in the investment account?
scenes.say: Quick check. A forty percent investee earns a hundred thousand and pays thirty thousand of dividends. Change in the investment account? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, $28,000: forty thousand less twelve thousand.

videos.title: Paying more than book value
videos.take: Excess cost is assigned to undervalued assets, which are depreciated, and to goodwill, which isn't

scenes.say: Suppose Bluestem had paid $700,000 for its thirty percent of Northshore, whose book net assets were $2 million.

scenes.heading: Assigning the excess
scenes.say: Bluestem's share of book value is $600,000, so it paid $100,000 extra. Northshore's equipment is undervalued by $200,000; Bluestem's thirty percent share is $60,000. The remaining $40,000 is goodwill.

scenes.heading: Investment income, 2031
scenes.say: The $60,000 assigned to equipment is depreciated over its ten-year remaining life, $6,000 a year, reducing investment income to $69,000. The goodwill isn't amortized.
None of this appears as separate equipment or goodwill on Bluestem's balance sheet. It's all inside the one-line investment account. That's why the equity method is called one-line consolidation.

sub: Test the whole investment if fair value
falls below carrying, other than temporarily
scenes.say: If the investment's fair value falls below its carrying amount and the decline is other than temporary, Bluestem writes it down. The write-down isn't reversed.

scenes.q: Share of investee income $50,000; excess cost assigned to equipment $30,000 over 5 years. Investment income?
scenes.say: Quick check. Share of investee income fifty thousand; excess cost assigned to equipment thirty thousand over five years. Investment income? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Control and consolidation
videos.take: With control, combine the subsidiary's statements line by line and show the noncontrolling interest

scenes.say: Bluestem owns all of Northwind Canoe. That's control, and Northwind's books are consolidated with Bluestem's.

When an investor controls another company, usually by owning more than half the voting shares, it prepares consolidated statements: the parent and subsidiary combined line by line as one economic entity.
If Bluestem owned eighty percent, the other twenty percent would be a noncontrolling interest, shown within equity, with its share of income shown separately.

Control can also come through contracts rather than votes. A variable interest entity is consolidated by the party that directs its key activities and absorbs its losses or benefits. This closed a big off-balance-sheet route.
Consolidation mechanics, eliminating intercompany sales and balances, are covered in advanced accounting. Here, know when it applies.

scenes.q: Bluestem owns 80% of a subsidiary. The other 20% is reported as:
scenes.say: Quick check. Bluestem owns eighty percent of a subsidiary. How is the other twenty percent reported? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, noncontrolling interest, within equity.

videos.title: Comparing the methods
videos.take: The same investee can produce very different investor income depending on the method

scenes.say: Same investee, same year, three methods. What would Bluestem report?

scenes.heading: Northshore: 30% share
scenes.say: Under fair value, Bluestem would report $24,000 of dividend revenue plus any change in the shares' fair value. Under the equity method, $75,000 of investment income. Under consolidation, all of Northshore's revenues and expenses, less a noncontrolling interest.
Companies can elect the fair value option for equity-method investments, reporting changes in fair value in income instead.

scenes.heading: Disclosures for equity-method investees
items: Difference between cost and underlying equity
scenes.say: For significant equity-method investees, disclose the name and ownership percentage, the difference between carrying amount and underlying equity, quoted fair value if available, and summarized financial information.
Because methods produce different income, managers sometimes structure stakes around the thresholds. Analysts focus on influence, not just the percentage.

scenes.q: Under the equity method, dividends received are:
scenes.say: Quick check. Under the equity method, dividends received are treated how? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, a reduction of the investment.

case: Bluestem owns 18% of Lakes Paddle Co. (cost $360,000, fair value now $390,000) with no board seat. It can buy another 7% for $150,000 and get a board seat. Lakes Paddle earns about $400,000 a year, pays $100,000 in dividends, and its share price swings widely. The founder wants to buy 'so we can report a share of their profit instead of the swings'.
Income under the current method if fair value rises $30,000 and dividends are $18,000.
Income under the equity method after the purchase (25% share).
Is the founder's reasoning a valid basis for the decision?
What determines the method after the purchase?

Current: 18,000 + 30,000 = 48,000 (volatile). Equity method: 25% × 400,000 = 100,000 (less amortization of any excess). The decision should rest on strategy and value, not reporting; the method follows significant influence (board seat, 25%), not preference.
exam: Explain how the level of influence determines the accounting for equity investments, and describe each method.
Little influence: FV-NI (or measurement alternative); significant: equity method (share of income, dividends reduce, excess amortized); control: consolidation with NCI.
Record Bluestem's 30% investment in Northshore: cost $700,000; book value $2,000,000; equipment undervalued $200,000 (10 years); income $250,000; dividends $80,000.
Excess 100,000: equipment 60,000, goodwill 40,000. Income 75,000 − 6,000 = 69,000; dividends 24,000; ending investment 745,000.
